title: Private deployments: VPC & On-prem reference, packaging, day-2 ops, upgrade/rollback, customer requirements
author: Daniel Kim
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference guidance for Private Deployments (VPC and on-prem). It covers recommended reference architectures, on-prem packaging and installation artifacts, a step-by-step VPC deployment guide, day-2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling), and upgrade/rollback procedures. The goal is a repeatable, audit-friendly playbook to satisfy security-sensitive customers and reduce operational risk during deploys and upgrades.

Scope and audience

- Audience: Solutions Engineers, Platform Engineers, Customer Infra teams, and SREs operating private deployments.
- Scope: VPC-hosted private control plane + optional on-prem runtime, fully air-gapped on-prem installs, and hybrid architectures. Includes pre-reqs, example network/topology diagrams, packaging notes, operational runbook steps, and rollback guidance.

Ownership and SLAs

- Owner: eng-private-deployments
- Primary contacts: Daniel Kim (author), Maya Patel (SRE reviewer), Alex Johnson (security reviewer)
- Operational SLA expectations: 99.9% control-plane availability for Dedicated Private customers; runtime SLOs depend on customer hardware - recommend documenting per-customer SLO in the contract.

TL;DR recommendations

- For regulated customers, prefer VPC deployment with private control plane and customer-managed subnets.
- Use the Hybrid reference (control plane in VPC, runtime on-prem) when low network latency to customer data is required.
- For air-gapped customers, use the on-prem bundle with signed images and offline package server; follow the packaging checklist.
- Always follow the precheck checklist before upgrades and run canary rollouts for model/runtime updates.

Reference architectures (summary)

1) VPC-hosted private control plane (recommended for most enterprise customers)

- Components: Control plane (Redwood-managed or customer-managed within customer VPC), Runtime fleet (customer/private VPC), Internal load balancer, NAT/egress gateway, Private DNS, KMS integration via VPC endpoint.
- Network layout: Separate subnets for control-plane, runtime, management, and monitoring. Use security groups and NACLs to enforce least privilege.

2) Hybrid: Control plane in customer VPC, runtime on-prem

- Use a secure transit (VPN or Direct Connect/ExpressRoute) with private peering for model artifacts and telemetry.
- Dataflow: requests -> customer LB -> runtime nodes (on-prem) -> optional control plane for model/metric sync.

3) Air-gapped on-prem deployment (regulated or classified environments)

- All artifacts delivered as signed tarballs and container images hosted on customer internal registry.
- No external egress permitted. Use air-gap upgrade bundles and an approved offline installer.

On-prem packaging and release artifacts

- Release artifact types: container images (OCI), helm charts (if k8s), operator bundle, offline tarball (signed), and package manifest (sha256 checksums).
- Image signing: All production images are signed with Redwood image signing key; customers should verify signatures on intake.
- Versioning: semantic (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and include build metadata; release notes must include migration notes and DB schema changes.
- KMS/HSM: We provide optional integrations with AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, and customer HSM certificates. Keys are never stored in plain text in artifacts.

Pre-deployment customer requirements checklist (summary)

- Network:
  - VPCs/subnets allocated: control-plane subnet, runtime subnet(s), management subnet
  - CIDR ranges (no overlap with customer on-prem for hybrid deployments)
  - Required ports: 443 (control plane), 10250 (kubelet, if k8s runtime), 2379/2380 (etcd, if applicable), 9090 (Prometheus scrape), 514/udp (syslog optional)
- Security:
  - IAM roles/service principals created with least privilege
  - KMS/HSM access provisioned (vault credentials)
  - Firewall rules and NACLs documented and approved
- Storage & hardware:
  - Persistent volumes (size and IOPS requirements documented per workload)
  - GPU count and type (for runtime): e.g., 4x A100-80GB per node for high throughput, or T4s for cost-sensitive workloads
- Observability:
  - Metrics endpoints reachable from the monitoring subnet
  - Log ingress (syslog or fluentd) and retention policy agreed
- Compliance:
  - Data residency and retention requirements documented
  - Audit log forwarder configured to customer SIEM if required

Detailed VPC deployment guide (step-by-step)

1) Prepare infrastructure
   - Create VPC and subnets: control-plane-subnet (private), runtime-subnet(s), management-subnet.
   - Ensure NAT/gateway/EIP for outbound artifact fetch (unless air-gapped).
   - Reserve Elastic IPs for public ingress (if required).

2) IAM and networking
   - Create IAM roles/service principals for the Redwood control-plane components, grant least privilege to S3/Blob storage buckets used for artifacts.
   - Create security groups: control-plane, runtime, monitoring. Only open required ports.

3) DNS and certificates
   - Configure private DNS zones for control-plane endpoints; issue TLS certs via customer CA or Redwood can provide certs if permitted.
   - Verify cert chains and CA trust on customer hosts.

4) Storage and artifact locations
   - Provision object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) for artifacts and model hosting, with lifecycle policies.
   - Ensure the control-plane has read access and runtime has read access to model artifacts.

5) Install control plane
   - For customer-managed control plane, follow the control-plane install: deploy operator, apply CRDs, and configure secret backends (KMS integration).
   - Validate API endpoints: curl https://control-plane.internal/api/health -> 200 OK.

6) Install runtime (Kubernetes or dedicated hosts)
   - Kubernetes: apply helm chart (values.yaml provided in bundle). Example: `helm upgrade --install redwood-runtime ./charts/runtime -f values.yaml --namespace redwood`.
   - Dedicated hosts (non-k8s): run runtime installer tarball and register agents with control plane using the registration token.

7) Validation and smoke tests
   - Smoke test checklist: control-plane health, runtime registration (agents list), sample inference request, Prometheus metrics visible, logs shipping to customer log collector.
   - Run 5 minute end-to-end test: send load that mimics production percentiles.

Day-2 operations (monitoring, alerting, scaling, backups)

Monitoring and observability
- Metrics: token-latency percentiles, request success rate, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate. Typical dashboards: per-model latency, per-node GPU/CPU/memory, per-route cost.
- Alerts (examples):
  - Control plane 5m error rate > 1% -> paged to oncall
  - Runtime node GPU memory > 90% for 2m -> page SRE
  - Failed model downloads > 3 within 15m -> trigger incident playbook

Backups and DR
- Backup schedule: etcd and postgres (if used) daily full backups, WAL shipping enabled. Store backups in customer-managed encrypted object storage.
- Restore window objective: RTO 2 hours, RPO 1 hour (adjust per customer contractual requirements).

Scaling and capacity management
- Autoscaling: Configure runtime autoscalers (K8s HPA/CA or custom GPU autoscaler). Provide recommended thresholds: scale-up when average GPU utilization > 75% for 3m.
- Capacity planning: Use 95th percentile tokens/sec by model for sizing; include warm-up capacity for cold starts.

Routine maintenance and security patching
- Patch cadence: minor security patches applied monthly under maintenance windows; major runtime upgrades follow the upgrade playbook below.
- Maintenance window runbook: notify customer 72h in advance, run canaries, validate health, then rollout to remainder in waves.

Upgrade and rollback procedures (runtime & control plane)

Pre-upgrade checks
1) Validate backup completeness (etcd/postgres and object storage).
2) Ensure canary environment or subset of nodes available for early rollout.
3) Validate that the new release has been smoke tested in staging with the same artifact signing and checksum verification.
4) Confirm maintenance window and stakeholder approvals.

Canary rollout procedure
1) Deploy new control-plane version to 1 canary replica (or single AZ) and run smoke tests for 30-60 minutes.
2) Deploy new runtime agent to a small subset (5-10%) of nodes or dedicated canary nodes.
3) Route a limited percentage (5-10%) of production traffic to the canary runtime using traffic split config in the control plane.
4) Monitor: latency P95, error rate, GPU failures, memory OOMs, and model output quality signals for at least 1 hour.

Full rollout and verification
1) If canary passes, incrementally roll out to remaining nodes in waves (e.g., 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with health checks between waves.
2) After each wave, run validation queries and automated evals tied to production prompt sets.

Rollback steps (if canary or rollout fails)
1) Immediately revert traffic routing to the previous version at the control-plane layer.
2) If control-plane change caused failure, redeploy previous control-plane version from signed artifacts and restore DB snapshot if necessary (use the backup from before upgrade).
3) If runtime agents failed, drain affected nodes (cordon + evict), redeploy previous agent version, and reintroduce nodes after health checks.
4) Post-incident: open a regression triage ticket and capture artifacts (logs, core dumps, traces).

Commands and snippets (examples)
- Verify control plane health:
  curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/health || exit 1

- Helm install example (k8s runtime):
  helm upgrade --install redwood-runtime ./charts/runtime -f values-prod.yaml --namespace redwood --wait --timeout 10m

- Agent registration (non-k8s):
  ./redwood-agent install --token $REG_TOKEN --control-plane https://control-plane.internal --kms-provider aws-kms

Customer requirements library (checklists by customer tier)

- Tier 1 (Regulated / Enterprise):
  - Air-gap support or private VPC, HSM/KMS integration, SIEM integration for audit logs, 12 month log retention option, formal SOC2 report exchange.
- Tier 2 (Large commercial):
  - Private VPC, encrypted artifact storage, automated backups, monthly scheduled maintenance windows.
- Tier 3 (SMB / Developer):
  - VPC with minimal isolation, standard observability, quarterly maintenance windows.

Acceptance and handoff checklist (before handover to customer ops)

- All predeployment checklist items verified and signed off.
- Smoke tests and E2E tests passed (document test results).
- Monitoring dashboards created and shared with customer teams.
- Runbooks and escalation playbooks provided to customer (oncall contact list, escalation tree).

Security and compliance notes

- Audit logs: All control-plane API actions are logged and exported to the customer SIEM on request.
- Data residency: Model artifact storage can be restricted to the customer region. Support DLP scanning on customer request.
- Secrets: Use ephemeral tokens for agent registration and rotate signing keys quarterly.

Related pages and artifacts

- Link to control-plane install guide: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-control-plane-install-2026-04-01
- Link to runtime helm charts and values: /repo/internal/charts/redwood-runtime (internal)

Appendix: common troubleshooting scenarios

1) Runtime nodes not registering
- Check network: can the node reach control-plane on 443?
- Check agent logs: `/var/log/redwood/agent.log` for registration errors and token expiration.

2) Model download failures
- Verify object storage permission/policy and signed URL validity.
- Check artifact manifest checksum: sha256 mismatch indicates corrupted artifact.

3) High tail latency after upgrade
- Re-run smoke tests against canary; compare model warm cache state. Consider immediate rollback if latency regressions persist for >30 minutes.

If you have questions or need a customer-specific variant of this playbook (e.g., custom firewall rules, specific GPU SKUs), contact eng-private-deployments@redwood.com or open a support ticket with `#private-deployments` in Slack.
